name: Incident Response Management
blurb: When prevention fails: the response lifecycle, forensics, malware analysis, hunting, and learning from every incident.

modules.title: Response Lifecycle
modules.blurb: From preparation to lessons learned: how incidents are run, contained, and closed.

topics.title: The Incident Response Lifecycle
topics.description: Preparation through lessons learned: the six phases every analyst runs, in order.
what: Incident response follows a lifecycle: Preparation (plans, playbooks, tools, training), Detection and Analysis (find and scope), Containment (stop the spread), Eradication (remove the cause), Recovery (restore safely), and Lessons Learned (improve). NIST SP 800-61 is the reference model.
Each phase has an exit before the next begins: you do not eradicate what you have not contained, and you do not recover what you have not eradicated.
why: Every IR scenario question is secretly asking which phase you are in and what that phase permits. Knowing the order answers containment-vs-eradication-vs-recovery questions instantly.

concepts.text: Plans, playbooks, roles, tools, and tabletop rehearsals before anything happens.
Confirming alerts, scoping impact, and declaring incidents.
Short-term isolation to stop spread; long-term holds for sustained operations.
Removing causes and vulnerabilities, then restoring and monitoring.
Post-incident review improving people, process, and tooling.

topics.example: Ransomware hits file shares at 2 AM. Preparation pays off: the on-call analyst opens the ransomware playbook instead of improvising — isolate first, then eradicate, then recover from clean backups, then review.

scenario.title: 2 AM ransomware
scenario.story: Help desk reports encrypted file shares spreading across departments. The ransomware playbook is on the shelf.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Rapidly spreading encryption, ransom notes appearing.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Active ransomware incident, not a drill.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Patient zero, encryption scope, C2 callbacks, backup integrity.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Lateral movement confirmed via SMB; backups appear clean.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Declare a major incident and run the playbook.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Contain (isolate segments), eradicate, recover from backups, review.

technical.title: Phase gates
technical.text: Never skip forward — each gate protects the next phase.

code.text:
PREPARE  -> playbooks, roles, tools, tabletops
DETECT  -> validate, scope, declare
CONTAIN -> isolate short-term, hold long-term
ERADICATE -> remove malware, close holes
RECOVER -> restore, harden, monitor
LEARN   -> review, fix process, update playbooks

exam: Phase order never changes: contain before eradicate before recover.
Tabletops and playbooks belong to preparation.
Post-incident improvement is always lessons learned.

confusions.text: Containment stops spread; eradication removes the cause.
Recovery restores operations; lessons learned improves the process afterward.
Events are observable occurrences; incidents are events needing response.

keyTerms.def: Six-phase model from preparation to lessons learned.
keyTerms.example: Running ransomware by the playbook.
Ransomware isolation steps at 2 AM.

keyTerms.def: Formal decision that an event is an incident.
keyTerms.example: Named staff declaring a major incident.

mistakes: Eradicating before containing — the threat spreads mid-cleanup.
Recovering from dirty backups.
Skipping lessons learned and repeating the incident.
examTips: Phase-order questions are free points if memorized.
Tabletop and playbook always signal preparation.
Anything post-incident improvement signals lessons learned.
topics.takeaway: Run incidents in phase order — prepare, detect, contain, eradicate, recover, learn — and never skip a gate.

checks.q: Malware is spreading. After detection, what comes first?
checks.explain: Stop the spread before removing causes.

checks.q: Tabletops and playbooks belong to which phase?

topics.title: Containment, Eradication, Recovery
topics.description: Isolate without breaking the business, remove causes completely, and restore with confidence.
what: Containment stops bleeding: short-term isolation (unplug, firewall block, disable account) buys time; long-term containment (segmented VLANs, monitored access) sustains operations during long incidents. Eradication removes malware, attacker accounts, persistence, and the exploited weakness. Recovery restores systems from known-clean backups, re-hardens, patches, and monitors closely for return.
Business impact shapes every choice: containing a business-critical server means surgical isolation that preserves evidence, not yanking power.
why: Analysts constantly choose between fast-but-destructive and slow-but-safe. The exam tests whether you contain first, preserve evidence, and restore only from clean sources.

concepts.text: Immediate isolation versus sustained monitored separation.
Memory, logs, and images captured before wiping anything.
Malware plus persistence plus entry point — all three, or it returns.
Restore from verified-clean backups, then patch and monitor.
Isolating by network zones to bound blast radius.

topics.example: Business-critical server shows malware. Instead of shutdown, the analyst isolates its switch port (network contained, memory preserved), images RAM, kills persistence, patches the entry flaw, then restores data from a verified backup.

scenario.title: The server that cannot die
scenario.story: Malware is confirmed on the ERP server at month-end close. Finance says downtime costs millions per hour.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Active malware on a cannot-fail system.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Containment must be surgical, not a power cut.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Memory image, persistence mechanisms, entry vector, backup integrity.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: C2 active but data intact; clean backups exist from last night.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Isolate at network, preserve, eradicate, recover.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Port isolation, memory capture, persistence removal, patch, monitored restore.

code.text:
1. block malicious IPs/domains at firewall/proxy
2. disable compromised accounts, revoke sessions
3. isolate host (EDR) or switch port, keep powered
4. segment network zones around the outbreak
5. full shutdown — last resort, evidence first

exam: Critical server plus malware means contain and preserve evidence — not shutdown or wipe.
Recovery demands verified-clean backups plus monitoring.
Eradication must include the entry point or reinfection follows.

confusions.text: Isolation cuts network while preserving memory; shutdown kills volatile evidence.
Eradication removes threats; recovery restores service.
Short-term buys hours; long-term sustains operations during long fights.

keyTerms.def: Stopping incident spread with minimal business harm.
keyTerms.example: EDR-isolating the ERP server.

keyTerms.def: Complete removal of threat plus root cause.
keyTerms.example: Killing persistence and patching the entry flaw.
Last night's offline backup set.

mistakes: Shutting down critical hosts before memory capture.
Wiping before removing persistence and entry points.
Recovering from untested backups.
examTips: Critical plus infected equals isolate and preserve.
Evidence before wiping, always.
Recovery answers mention clean backups plus monitoring.
topics.takeaway: Contain surgically, eradicate completely, recover only from clean — in that order.

checks.q: Malware on a business-critical server. First move?
checks.explain: Surgical containment protects business and forensics.

options: Malware, persistence, and entry point are gone
checks.answer: Malware, persistence, and entry point are gone
checks.explain: All three, or it comes back.
Dirty restores reinfect; watch for return.

modules.title: Forensics and Malware Analysis
modules.blurb: Evidence that holds up and malware safely detonated: imaging, hashing, sandboxes.

topics.title: Digital Forensics Essentials
topics.description: Order of volatility, imaging, hashing, chain of custody, and write blockers — evidence that holds up.
what: Forensics answers what happened using defensible evidence. Collect in order of volatility: memory and running processes first (gone at power-off), then disk, then logs. Image drives bit-for-bit through write blockers that prevent alteration, hash original and copy (matching hashes prove integrity), and document every handler in the chain of custody.
Legal hold freezes relevant data from deletion when litigation is possible.
why: One wrong move — imaging without a write blocker, rebooting before memory capture — destroys admissibility. Exam questions test exactly these failure points.

concepts.text: Memory, processes first; disk, then logs, then archives.
Hardware/software preventing writes during imaging.
Matching MD5/SHA hashes proving the copy equals the original.
Documented handling log from seizure to courtroom.
Preservation order suspending normal deletion.

topics.example: Suspected rogue employee's drive: analyst images through a write blocker, hashes both (match), logs every access. When hashes later mismatch on a re-image, the cause is clear — imaging altered it, so evidence handling failed.

scenario.title: The mismatched hash
scenario.story: Initial drive hash does not match the imaged copy's hash. Counsel is asking questions.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Hash mismatch between original and image.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: The imaging process itself altered data.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Imaging method, write-blocker usage logs, handler records.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: No write blocker was used — the OS wrote during imaging.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Evidence integrity compromised by procedure.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Re-image correctly with blocker, document the failure, retrain.

code.text:
1. photograph screen + note running state
2. capture memory (winpmem / LiME) BEFORE power-off
3. image disk via write blocker
4. hash original + image, compare
5. bag, tag, chain-of-custody log

exam: Hash mismatch after imaging means no write blocker was used.
Memory before power-off — volatility order is law.
Legal hold preserves data when litigation looms.

confusions.text: Imaging is bit-for-bit including slack; copying misses hidden data.
Custody tracks handling; hold prevents deletion.
Match proves integrity; mismatch proves alteration somewhere.

keyTerms.def: Device preventing any writes to evidence media.
keyTerms.example: USB blocker during drive imaging.

keyTerms.def: Who handled evidence, when, and why.
keyTerms.example: Signed log from seizure to lab.
RAM before disk before logs.

mistakes: Imaging without a write blocker.
Rebooting before memory capture.
Skipping hash verification.
examTips: Mismatch equals missing write blocker.
Volatility order questions are free points.
Legal hold appears with HR and litigation context.
topics.takeaway: Volatile first, image through blockers, hash everything, log every hand.

checks.q: Imaged hash differs from original. Cause?

topics.title: Malware Analysis
topics.description: Static versus dynamic analysis, sandboxes, and safe detonation — learning what malware does without becoming the victim.
what: Static analysis examines malware without running it: hashes, strings, headers, and imports reveal capabilities cheaply and safely. Dynamic analysis runs it in an isolated sandbox (Cuckoo, Joe Sandbox) and watches behavior: files dropped, registry keys, C2 callbacks.
Analysts start static for triage, detonate the interesting ones, and never run samples on production or personal machines.
why: Phishing attachments and EDR alerts constantly demand a verdict: malicious or benign? Analysis gives the answer with evidence instead of guesses.

concepts.text: No-execution inspection: strings, hashes, headers.
Sandboxed execution observing real behavior.
Isolated detonation chamber with full monitoring.
Readable text inside binaries hinting at function.
Malware phoning home — the behavior that condemns it.

topics.example: Suspicious Invoice PDF arrives: strings show no scripts (fast static triage), but policy says detonate — Cuckoo shows it dropping an executable and beaconing. Verdict: malicious, with a behavior report attached.

scenario.title: Invoice or infection?
scenario.story: User forwards Invoice-0489293348.pdf from an unknown sender asking if it is safe.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Unsolicited PDF with urgent open-me language.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Possible targeted phishing payload.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Static strings plus full sandbox detonation trace.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Sandbox shows dropped exe plus C2 beacons.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Malicious — customized for the recipient.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Block hashes and C2, hunt for other recipients, brief the user.

technical.title: Safe analysis ladder
technical.text: Climb only as far as the question needs.

code.text:
# 1. identify (never execute yet)
file Invoice-0489293348.pdf
sha256sum Invoice-0489293348.pdf
# 2. static peek
strings Invoice-0489293348.pdf | grep -iE 'cmd|powershell|http'
# 3. detonate ONLY in sandbox:
# cuckoo submit Invoice-0489293348.pdf  (isolated VM)

exam: Customized attachment impact means detonate in sandbox (Cuckoo), not strings alone.
Static is safe and fast; dynamic reveals behavior.
Never analyze on production — sandbox only.

confusions.text: Static inspects without running; dynamic runs isolated and watches.
Sandboxes detonate known samples; honeypots attract unknown attackers.
Strings hint; only behavior confirms.

keyTerms.def: Isolated VM for safe malware execution.
keyTerms.example: Cuckoo detonating the invoice PDF.
Strings revealing powershell hints.
C2 beacons in the sandbox trace.

mistakes: Opening samples on workstations to see what happens.
Stopping at strings when behavior is the question.
Skipping detonation for targeted attachments.
examTips: Customized attachment equals sandbox detonation.
Behavior questions want dynamic analysis.
Sandbox names to recognize: Cuckoo, Joe Sandbox.
topics.takeaway: Static to triage, sandbox to convict — and never detonate outside isolation.

checks.q: Best way to judge a customized attachment's impact?
checks.explain: Behavior in isolation gives the verdict.

checks.q: Strings output is an example of?

modules.title: Hunting and Exercises
modules.blurb: Threat hunting hypotheses plus tabletop rehearsals and lessons that actually improve.

topics.title: Threat Hunting
topics.description: Hypothesis-driven hunts with ATT&CK: finding attackers your detections missed.
what: Threat hunting proactively searches for hidden adversaries using hypotheses: if attackers use technique X, evidence Y should exist in our data. Hunters pivot through ATT&CK-mapped telemetry — process trees, auth logs, DNS — confirming or killing each hypothesis.
Hunting differs from alert triage: no alert fired. The hunter starts from intel, anomalies, or crown-jewel risk and goes looking.
why: Advanced attackers evade signatures. Hunting is how SOCs catch them anyway — and exam questions test whether you know hunting starts with a hypothesis, not an alert.

concepts.text: Testable prediction guiding the hunt.
Framing hunts around adversary techniques.
Moving from one indicator to related data.
Highest-value assets worth hunting around first.
Proactive searching versus reactive alert handling.

topics.example: Intel reports credential dumping via LSASS access. Hypothesis: LSASS accessed outside approved tools. Hunt: EDR process data for non-approved LSASS handles — two hosts light up, and an incident begins.

scenario.title: Hunt the dumper
scenario.story: No alerts, but threat intel says your sector faces LSASS credential dumping.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Nothing — that is the point of hunting.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: If dumpers ran, LSASS anomalies exist in EDR data.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Process access events to LSASS, approved-tool allowlist.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Two hosts show unknown processes reading LSASS.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Hypothesis confirmed — convert hunt to incident.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Isolate hosts, collect memory, expand timeline.

technical.title: Hunt loop
technical.text: Every hunt follows the same cycle.

code.text:
INTEL/ANOMALY -> hypothesis (ATT&CK technique)
  -> collect telemetry (EDR, auth, DNS)
  -> analyze (confirm or kill hypothesis)
  -> confirmed? open incident : document + new hypothesis

exam: Hunting starts from hypotheses or intel — never from an alert.
ATT&CK frames hunts around techniques.
Confirmed hunts become incidents with isolation first.

confusions.text: Hunting seeks hidden threats proactively; triage reacts to fired alerts.
Hypotheses start hunts; alerts start triage.
Hunt around highest value first — time is finite.

keyTerms.example: LSASS-access hunt from fresh intel.
If dumpers ran, EDR shows it.

keyTerms.def: Expanding from one finding to related data.
keyTerms.example: Bad IP to all hosts that called it.

mistakes: Waiting for alerts instead of hunting.
Hunting without a hypothesis — fishing, not hunting.
Skipping documentation of killed hypotheses.
examTips: No alert plus proactive search equals hunting.
Hypothesis wording reveals hunt questions.
ATT&CK appears in hunt framing.
topics.takeaway: Hunt with hypotheses, pivot with data, convert confirmations to incidents.

topics.title: Tabletops and Lessons Learned
topics.description: Rehearsing incidents with tabletops, then converting every incident into improvement.
what: Tabletop exercises walk stakeholders through a fictional scenario — ransomware at quarter-end, a leaked database — to test plans, roles, and decisions without real damage. Executives, legal, comms, and IT discover gaps together.
Lessons learned close real incidents: what worked, what failed, which playbooks change, which controls get funded. Metrics (MTTD/MTTR trends) prove improvement.
why: Prepared teams outperform heroic ones. Exam questions treat tabletops as preparation and lessons learned as the mandatory ending — mixing them with response phases is a classic trap.

concepts.text: Discussion-based rehearsal with cross-functional players.
Structured diffuse of what happened and why.
Converting lessons into changed procedures.
Metrics showing whether response actually improves.
Legal, comms, executives — responders plus deciders.

topics.example: CISO tabletops a ransomware scenario with the comms chief: who approves the press statement, and when? The gap found in the room beats discovering it at 2 AM.

scenario.title: The statement nobody approved
scenario.story: Tabletop: customer data is leaked on a Friday night. Reporters call Saturday morning.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Simulated leak plus media pressure.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Comms approval chain is the likely gap.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Who drafts, who approves, how fast, per the plan.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: No pre-approved holding statement exists.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Gap confirmed without real damage.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: Draft holding statements, name approvers, re-exercise quarterly.

code.text:
0:00  scenario inject (what just happened)
0:20  response walk (who does what, in what order)
0:45  comms + legal inject (statement? disclosure?)
1:05  gaps + owners + deadlines
1:20  schedule the re-exercise

exam: Tabletop questions are preparation-phase questions.
After any incident or exercise, next is lessons learned.
Comms officers join tabletops for press-handling reasons.

confusions.text: Tabletops discuss; live-fire exercises execute technically.
Recovery restores service; lessons improve the machine.
After-actions fix process; blame fixes nothing.

keyTerms.example: Friday-night leak with the comms chief.
New holding statements after the exercise.
Falling MTTR proving the program works.

mistakes: Running tabletops with only IT in the room.
Filing lessons learned without owners or deadlines.
Confusing exercises with real response phases.
examTips: Tabletop equals preparation, always.
Post-anything improvement equals lessons learned.
Comms chief presence signals press-handling.
topics.takeaway: Rehearse with tabletops, improve with lessons learned, prove it with trends.

checks.q: After a tabletop, what comes next?
Why invite the comms chief to a tabletop?
Best proof the IR program improves?

modules.title: Insider Threats and Sensitive Investigations
modules.blurb: UEBA signals, HR-safe evidence handling, and privacy-compliant investigation.

topics.title: Insider Threat Investigations
topics.description: Detecting malicious insiders with UEBA and investigating them without violating privacy or HR policy.
what: Insider threats come from employees, contractors, or partners misusing legitimate access — maliciously (theft, sabotage) or negligently. UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics) baselines normal behavior and flags anomalies: impossible hours, mass downloads, privilege creep.
Investigations touching HR matters demand extra care: minimize identifiable data, password-protect evidence, restrict access to need-to-know personnel, and coordinate with HR and legal early.
why: Insider cases combine technical investigation with legal landmines. The exam tests both: recognizing UEBA signals AND handling evidence in HR-compliant ways.

concepts.text: Behavior baselines flagging anomalous user activity.
Intent matters for response: sabotage versus mistakes.
Restricting sensitive case access to essential personnel.
Removing identifiers from case materials where possible.
Preserving data when action may follow.

topics.example: UEBA flags a finance user downloading ten times their normal volume at 3 AM. The analyst quietly verifies with proxy logs, loops in HR and legal, and secures evidence with restricted access — no broadcast, no tipping off.

scenario.title: The terminable click
scenario.story: A user accessed a banned site — a terminable offense. The SOC must build a case that survives HR and privacy scrutiny.

walkthrough.label: Observed activity
walkthrough.text: Policy violation with employment consequences.

walkthrough.label: Initial hypothesis
walkthrough.text: Evidence must be airtight and compliant.

walkthrough.label: Evidence to collect
walkthrough.text: Auth logs, web logs, workstation temp files showing searches.

walkthrough.label: Analysis
walkthrough.text: Activity confirmed across independent sources.

walkthrough.label: Decision
walkthrough.text: Build an HR-safe case, not just a technical one.

walkthrough.label: Next action
walkthrough.text: De-identified details, password-protected evidence, restricted access, HR coordination.

technical.title: HR-safe evidence checklist
technical.text: Every sensitive case gets these protections.

code.text:
[x] minimize user-identifiable details in case notes
[x] password-protect evidence files
[x] restrict access to investigation personnel only
[x] coordinate HR + legal before confrontation
[x] full timeline: dates, accounts, hosts, IPs

exam: HR/privacy investigations demand de-identification plus protected, restricted evidence.
UEBA plus anomaly equals insider-threat detection.
Timelines with dates, accounts, hosts, and IPs build cases.

confusions.text: UEBA learns behavior baselines; SIEM rules match fixed patterns.
Intent differs; both need least-privilege prevention.
Hold preserves for action; deletion destroys cases.

keyTerms.example: 3 AM mass downloads by finance.
HR plus counsel only on the evidence.
User-123 instead of names in notes.

mistakes: Broadcasting suspect names before HR involvement.
Collecting evidence without privacy safeguards.
Confronting users before the case is built.
examTips: HR context always means protect and restrict evidence.
UEBA plus odd hours equals insider investigation.
Timelines win cases: dates, accounts, hosts, IPs.
topics.takeaway: Catch insiders with behavior analytics; prosecute them with HR-safe evidence.

checks.q: UEBA flags 3 AM mass downloads. This suggests?
checks.explain: Anomalous user behavior is UEBA's signal.
